INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici are social scientists whose research centers
on American elections and citizenship.2
D. Sunshine Hillygus, PhD, is a political scientist professor and researcher at Duke University who
has focused on the topics of American political behavior, campaigns and elections, survey methods, public
opinion, and information technology and politics.
Kevin T. Morris, PhD,  is a senior research fellow and voting policy scholar at the Brennan Center
for Justice, where he focuses on voting rights, election
administration, and the effects of the criminal justice
system on political participation.
Susan J. Pearson, PhD, is a researcher and professor of history at Northwestern University of the
nineteenth- and early twentieth-century United
States. She focuses on the cultural politics of reform,

INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Congress enacted two commonsense safeguards
when it passed the National Voter Registration Act of
1993 (NVRA). To determine a voter’s eligibility to
vote, a state should only ask a voter for essential information. Then, when a federal election is around the
corner — that is, less than 90 days away — a voter
should be able to focus on voting, not fixing their registration. These safeguards ensure that states can
“enforce [voting] requirements” while “increasing the
number of eligible citizens who register to vote in elections for Federal office.” Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Ariz., 570 U.S. 1, 13–17 (2013) (quoting 52 U.S.C.
§ 20501(b)(1)). Respect for these safeguards is the law,
which the Ninth Circuit correctly applied. Amici submit this brief to provide the Court with research that
shows how, and why, these safeguards matter for voters: They provide predictable, reasonable rules that
prevent administrative burdens, costs, and confusion
from wrongfully disenfranchising voters as an election
approaches.
1. Research supports one of Congress’s primary
findings underpinning the NVRA: “unfair registration
laws and procedures can have a direct and damaging
effect on voter participation[.]” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20501(a)(3). That research estimates that 21 million
voters do not have ready access to documentary proof

3

of citizenship, likely due in part to the costs and burdens that voters face in obtaining and accessing such
documents. In addition, these burdens can disproportionately affect certain groups, such as Native Americans, married women, and young voters. Consistent
with this reality, under the NVRA, applicants filling
out the federal voter registration form need not submit documentary proof of citizenship. Instead, Congress specified that the federal voter registration form
require a voter to “aver, under penalty of perjury,”
that the voter “is a citizen.” Arizona, 570 U.S. at 4–5.
Relevant provisions of the NVRA govern registration processes for federal elections. As such, when Arizona voters use the state voter registration form, but
do not provide documentary proof of citizenship, the
NVRA ensures that they will still be registered for federal elections. That is because documentary proof of
citizenship is not “necessary,” or essential, for an election official to “assess the eligibility of the applicant,”
52 U.S.C. § 20508(b)(1), for federal registration, as the
Ninth Circuit correctly concluded. Pet.App.37a, 50a.
Arizona House Bill 2492, however, requires election
officials to categorically reject state-form applicants
who lack documentary proof of citizenship, rather
than register those applicants for federal elections.
See House Bill 2492, 55th Leg., 2d Reg. Sess. (Ariz.
2022); A.R.S. § 16-121.01(C) (implementing requirement). No evidence in the record below suggests why
this requirement is necessary. Nor could it. Congress’s
attestation requirement accords with similar attestation requirements in virtually every state. Simply put,
documentary proof of citizenship is not necessary to

4

verify a voter’s citizenship, and requiring it could severely burden — or  worse, disenfranchise entirely —
millions of eligible voters.
2. Research demonstrates that a voter wrongfully
removed from the rolls right before an election could
face substantial costs and be deterred or prevented
from voting altogether. Of course, states also have an
ongoing interest in “ensur[ing] that accurate and current voter registration rolls are maintained.”
52 U.S.C. § 20501(b)(4). The NVRA’s 90-Day Provision creates a careful framework to balance both sets
of interests. It requires states to complete, within 90
days of a federal election, “any program” that seeks
“to systematically remove the names of ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible voters.” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A) (emphases added).
Congress’s choice reflects what research bears
out: clear, predictable deadlines, such as cutoff dates
for registering voters and sending out ballots, effectively balance states’ election administration needs
with the needs of voters, candidates, and others involved in elections. But Arizona House Bill 2243 upends this careful balance to require election officials
to systematically remove suspected noncitizens from
the voting rolls on a monthly basis, including during
the 90-day period before an election. H.B. 2243, 55th
Leg., 2d Reg. Sess. (Ariz. 2022); see also A.R.S. § 16-
165(A)(10), (E)–(L).
Ultimately, this Court is called upon to decide a
“narrow issue narrowly[.]” Watson v. Republican Nat’l

5

Comm., 609 U.S. 672, 693 (2026).  It need not determine whether the NVRA prevents removals of ineligible voters; the NVRA allows states to do so. Nor need
it address whether an individual who is not a citizen
can be removed; under the NVRA, that person can be
removed. The only issue before the court is whether
Arizona can deploy a systematic program of removal
with fewer than 90 days before an election. The clear
terms set forth by Congress in the NVRA, along with
the devastating consequences that would fall upon eligible voters from such a program, make clear that Arizona cannot do so.
• • •
The Ninth Circuit applied the right reading of the
NVRA. This Court should affirm.
ARGUMENT
I. Evidence Shows That Millions of Eligible
Voters Lack Ready Access to Documentary
Proof of citizenship.
The Ninth Circuit correctly applied the plain
meaning of the NVRA when it concluded that documentary proof of citizenship is not “necessary” to “assess the eligibility of the applicant,” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20508(b)(1), for federal registration. Pet.App.37a,
50a. Petitioner has cited no evidence to the contrary.
There is, however, ample evidence of the harm that
requiring documentary proof of citizenship will inflict
upon eligible voters: research estimates that

6

approximately 21 million voters do not have ready access to such documents, likely due in part to the costs
and burdens they face in obtaining them.
The plain language of the NVRA limits states to
asking for “necessary” information when registering
voters for federal elections. See 52 U.S.C.
§§ 20505(a)(2) (requiring that a state’s voter registration form, when used to register voters for federal elections, must meet “all of the criteria” of the federal
form); 20508(b)(1) (limiting identifying information to
that “necessary” to assess a registrant’s eligibility). As

II. The 90-Day Provision of the NVRA Provides
a Clear Rule That Prevents Unnecessary
Voter Costs and Confusion.
No later than 90 days before a federal election, a
state must complete “any program” that purports to
“systematically remove the names of ineligible voters
from the official lists of eligible voters.” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A). By enacting this provision, Congress
both ensured that voter rolls are accurately maintained and encouraged procedures that will “enhance[] the participation of eligible citizens as voters
in election for Federal office.” Arcia v. Fla. Sec’y of
State, 772 F.3d 1335, 1346 (11th Cir. 2014).  This balance is far from unique: federal and state election laws
are replete with similar deadlines, such as cutoff dates
for registering voters and sending out ballots, that
balance states’ election administration needs with the
needs of voters, candidates, and others to plan their
pre-Election Day activities. A wealth of research affirms this approach, demonstrating that voters
wrongfully removed in the leadup to an election could
face undue costs and confusion that may impede or
deter them from voting altogether.

A. The 90-Day Provision Provides a Clear
Rule, Consistent with Countless Other
Election Deadlines, that Balances the
Needs of States and Voters in the Final
Days Before Election Day.
Congress struck a “careful balance” when it enacted the 90-Day Provision, permitting systematic removal programs at “any time except for the 90 days
before an election because that is when the risk of disfranchising eligible voters is the greatest.” Arcia, 772
F.3d at 1346. Before the 90-day window, a registrant
who has been incorrectly removed may have time to
correct any errors. Id. And within the 90-day window,
a registrant removed on an individualized basis has
usually been the subject of an individualized inquiry
or correspondence, reducing the chance of a mistake.
Id. But a systematic removal program — like that contemplated by H.B. 2243 — deployed within the 90-day
window creates the risk that eligible voters could be
removed right before Election Day with little time to
correct any errors. That is why courts have rejected
attempts to systematically remove registrants who
fall outside of Congress’s stated exceptions. See, e.g.,
Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1342 (blocking program attempting
to systematically remove suspected noncitizens
within 90-day period); N. Carolina State Conf. of
NAACP v. Bipartisan Bd. of Elections & Ethics Enf’t ,
No. 16-CV-1274, 2018 WL 3748172, *6–10 (M.D.N.C.
Aug. 7, 2018) (blocking removals from voter rolls without individualized inquiries within 90-day period);
Majority Forward v. Ben Hill Cnty. Bd. of Elections ,

512 F. Supp. 3d 1354, 1369–70 (M.D. Ga. 2021)

B. The 90-Day Provision Prevents Undue
Costs and Confusion for Voters.
Without the neutrally applicable election administration deadline that the 90-Day Provision guarantees, Arizona could initiate a last-minute, systematic
purge of its voter rolls that could lead to eligible voters
being erroneously removed from the rolls before Election Day. Ample research demonstrates the harm that
flows from such wrongful removals in the leadup to an
election — remedying issues with one’s voter registration requires significant time and imposes substantial
costs. Further, the mere possibility of status changes
right before Election Day  can deter voters from voting
altogether.
First, the 90-day Provision prevents an eligible
voter who is erroneously removed from being saddled
with last-minute costs and hurdles to remedy the mistake in time for Election Day. Under Arizona’s documentary proof-of-citizenship requirement, a voter erroneously deemed not to be a citizen may need to
provide a birth certificate, passport, naturalization
certificate or number, or tribal identification. See
A.R.S. § 16-166(F). And the process of obtaining such
documents, as discussed supra §I, often requires navigating confusing government websites, completing
detailed forms, and providing other forms of identification that may themselves be difficult to obtain. For
those without internet access, reliable transportation,
or flexible work schedules, even initiating the process
can be a major hurdle. Indeed, many voters must take
time off work or school to visit county or state offices,

36

which may be located far from home — particularly
for those in rural areas or tribal lands. Courts have
found persuasive survey estimates showing that, even
without Election Day right around the corner, such
documentation is burdensome, time-consuming, and
costly for individual Americans. 67 In short, obtaining
acceptable documents to establish citizenship costs
money and takes substantial time — both of which
may prove dispositive in determining whether a voter
can cast a ballot in an impending election.
Second, research suggests that having to obtain
these documents at the last minute undoubtedly affects voters’ cost-benefit calculus. Voting costs reflect
not only the direct financial costs of registration, but
also the time and effort required to overcome barriers
to participation. These costs are considerably higher
for young people and students, as discussed supra
§I.A.68
Fears that one lacks the right document or may
make a mistake in the process — fears that would be
heightened under both H.B. 2243 and H.B. 2492 —
can also deter voters from voting after an erroneous
removal. Notably, an empirical analysis of North

CONCLUSION
For more than 30 years, states across the country
have implemented the commonsense safeguards at issue in this case: they have required voters to provide
only essential information when they register to vote
and, as elections approach, ensured voters are not
wrongfully removed from the rolls. Congress struck a
deliberate balance between the needs of states and
voters when it designed these safeguards, and research demonstrates that they continue to be of vital
importance. The Ninth Circuit correctly upheld Congress’s protections, and amici respectfully urge this
Court to affirm its decision.
